cyber.title: Iran-linked intrusions into US water controllers
cyber.method: Break-ins to internet-exposed controllers at small water utilities, changing settings and locking out operators
cyber.summary: A new report says suspected Iranian hackers locked operators out of controls at small Midwest water stations and also breached two tankers bound for Texas. Intrusions have been reported in at least 12 states, with local rather than widespread service problems. US agencies earlier warned that Iran-affiliated actors altered controller logic.
cyber.us_why: The intrusions happened in US towns. US agencies urge utilities to take controllers off the open internet and change default passwords; no formal attribution has been made.
cyber.what_to_watch: A formal US attribution or a service outage affecting a larger city.

sources.text: The Wall Street Journal reports suspected Iranian hackers locked operators out of small-town Midwest water-station controls, breached two Texas-bound tankers and overheated hundreds of European store fridges since summer.

Science Times reports water-system intrusions across at least 12 US states; Iran-linked hackers are leading suspects, but no formal attribution, with localized rather than widespread service problems.
CSIS reports hackers hit more than 30 Minnesota water systems in July; in Georgia a pump station shutdown cut pressure and led to a boil-water advisory, with no illnesses reported.
CISA, FBI, NSA and EPA updated advisory AA26-097A on July 23, saying Iran-affiliated actors altered controller logic at US water utilities, in one case disabling shutdown and alarm functions.
Al Jazeera recalls a July attack on over 30 Minnesota water systems; the FBI and CISA warned of attacks in 12 states, with Iran-aligned hackers suspected, not confirmed.
NBC News reported on Sept 2, citing four sources, that Iranian hackers also tried to reach US telecom and energy systems. The attempts were reported as unsuccessful so far.
CSIS's incident list says the IRGC-linked CyberAv3ngers claimed the August water campaign across at least a dozen states. It says the US government had not publicly attributed it.

ABC News reported on Aug 4, citing sources, that water-sector intrusions reached at least 12 states, with Iran the prime suspect. Involvement was unconfirmed and supplies saw no widespread disruption.

cyber.summary: Lumen's Black Lotus Labs says the Chinese group Volt Typhoon used a relay network it calls Silent Train. Targets were mostly US government, defence and university networks. Sessions are short and tools are wiped afterward, which makes detection hard.
cyber.us_why: Lumen says US networks were the main targets, using TP-Link, Netgear and Fortinet devices sold in the US. The notes contain no new US government statement.
cyber.what_to_watch: A CISA or FBI advisory on Silent Train, or a takedown.

sources.text: BleepingComputer says Silent Train sessions are short, with tools wiped afterward, which makes detection hard. Lumen says it was partly a response to the FBI's earlier KV-botnet takedown.
Black Lotus Labs (Lumen) says Chinese group Volt Typhoon used a covert relay network, Silent Train, in four zero-day campaigns against management and edge systems.

Nextgov says Lumen found Silent Train targets mostly US government, defense and university networks, concentrated in Hawaii, California and Texas. It used TP-Link, Netgear and Fortinet devices also sold in the US.

cyber.title: Hacked supermarket fridges in Europe; France names Iranian suspects
cyber.method: Remote access to outdated refrigeration controllers, pushing temperatures up
cyber.summary: French judicial authorities attribute the attacks on refrigeration at hundreds of French stores to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, naming three Iranians and issuing international arrest warrants. A Nov 2 wave hit stores in at least eight European countries, including Ireland.

actor.name: Iran's Revolutionary Guards, per French judicial authorities

cyber.us_why: US agencies warned that cold-chain and refrigeration systems are being targeted and gave steps to secure them. The US has not formally named a culprit.
cyber.what_to_watch: Reports of similar fridge hacks at US stores or food warehouses.

sources.text: French judicial authorities attribute last month's attack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of French stores to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, naming three Iranians and issuing international arrest warrants, per a report relaying the WSJ.
RTÉ reports that on Monday Nov 2 refrigeration systems in at least eight European countries were hit, including 13 SuperValu stores in Ireland, with some set as high as 50C.

CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT issued a joint fact sheet warning that industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems are being targeted, with steps such as removing devices from the internet and changing default passwords.

TechCrunch says the US has not formally named a culprit, though researchers and reportedly US officials suspect Iran; affected units included Danfoss remote-control models whose maker had stopped security updates.
FoodNavigator, citing BBC, says the Nov 2-3 wave hit over 100 retailers in seven countries, apparently using the French method; its country count differs from BleepingComputer's six.
SC Media, citing Politico, says pro-Russian hacktivist groups claimed the European attacks while responsibility remains unconfirmed; this differs from Paris's reported blame on Iran's IRGC.

The advisory says attackers exploit unpatched or internet-exposed controllers via authentication bypass, code injection or weak setups to force continuous defrost; it urges removing them from the internet and changing default passwords.
The French blood service says a cold-storage vendor was hit, raising defrost and temperature limits; staff detected it in time to rescue blood samples.

boil.question: Will the Houthi–Saudi fighting widen into a clearly wider war, drawing in a new state or reopening attacks on Red Sea shipping?
boil.likelihood_of: a clearly wider war, with a new state joining or a new country's territory attacked, within 30 days
boil.summary: The Houthis keep firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia, and the Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh. On the ground, an unconfirmed report says the Houthis took the Kharaz base in Lahj, and some outlets say government forces left the Bab el-Mandeb area. No new attacks on ships have been reported, Riyadh airport has reopened, and no new state has joined the fighting.

ai_risk.summary: No development today clearly raised the near-term chance of catastrophic harm, and the picture is close to yesterday's. Cyber remains the most concrete risk: a Japan-led probe found servers likely used for AI-driven attacks, and the FBI's warning about the Artex tool keeps spreading. Two large US outages, at Microsoft and at the FAA, drew AI speculation, but officials say neither was caused by AI or a cyberattack, while US-China talks and UN talks in Geneva put AI safety and autonomous weapons on diplomatic agendas.

recent.text: The Abu Dhabi round is likely to go ahead on Nov 10-11, since both Moscow and Washington have confirmed delegations; past rounds produced prisoner swaps but no deal.
recent.why: The round went ahead, and Euronews reports it produced an agreement in principle on a prisoner exchange but no ceasefire or territorial deal. That matches the call as written.

recent.text: The Abu Dhabi round is likely to go ahead with modest results, given both delegations are named and Moscow says it offers no new concessions.
recent.why: The round took place and, per AP (via PBS), ended with a large prisoner exchange confirmed by both sides but no major breakthrough. The Moscow Times says neither side has shown major compromise.
